chunks: "At scale it becomes a systems problem: how many boards per hour can I test, at what cost, and how do I know the test itself is trustworthy.

For high volume you use fixtured test: a bed-of-nails in-circuit tester where hundreds of spring probes contact test pads at once, so a full structural test takes seconds, plus a fast functional test.
Boards go through on conveyors with automatic loading and unloading, and often several boards or a whole panel are tested in parallel.
You budget test time against the line's takt time; if the line makes a board every 30 seconds, the test cell needs to match, or you add test stations in parallel.

Cost-wise there's a crossover: a fixture might cost several thousand dollars but runs in seconds, while a flying probe has no fixture but takes minutes, so fixtures win above a certain volume, maybe a couple of thousand boards in an example.

Then there's data: every board gets a serial number, results are logged, and statistics on yield per station and per failure type feed back to the line, so if a feeder starts misplacing a part you see it in ICT failures within the hour.
Test systems are calibrated, and golden boards check that the tester still catches known faults.
For the design, I'd make this practical by adding test points on the nets that matter, on one side of the board, with fixture-friendly spacing, and boundary scan where pins are not accessible."
